title: Wandering Priest of the Apocalypse
description: Dialog nodes for Father Cain — a wandering preacher who carries a scorched pre-war Bible and a battered camp stove. He is not affiliated with the Church of the Atom, the Followers of the Apocalypse, or any organization he is aware of. He believes the bombs were a judgement, that the wasteland is a purgatory, and that the path forward requires the same virtues that were required before: charity, endurance, and not stealing other people's food. He dispenses wisdom with equal parts scripture and practical survival advice, and he is one of the genuinely kind people in the Mojave.
backstory: Ordained twice: once before the bombs, by a denomination that no longer exists; and once by himself, in the ruins of a Vegas wedding chapel, having concluded that the authority to minister could be self-granted when alternatives were unavailable. He has been walking a circuit of wasteland settlements for thirty years, offering what comfort can be given and what hard truths are necessary. His pre-war Bible has forty years of margin notes in four colors of scavenged pen.

intro.text:
Peace be with you, traveller.

I know. You're surprised. Most people out here don't lead with that.

My name is Father Cain — yes, like the biblical one. My mother had a sense of humour and a lot of faith that it would work out. Mostly it has.

I walk the Mojave. All of it, as far as I can manage. I offer what I can — medicine, food, a listening ear — and I ask nothing in return except that people extend the same courtesy to the next person they meet who needs it.

The world ended. The obligation to one another did not.
intro.video_speech: Peace be with you, traveller. My name is Father Cain. I know — like the biblical one. My mother had a sense of humour.

knowledge_nodes.text:
Captain Rex. I've passed through his checkpoint three times.

The second time he stopped me for twenty minutes. He wanted to know why I kept coming back to Freeside.

I told him: because that's where the people are who most need what I carry. He thought about that and let me through every time after.

Loxley the outlaw. He gave me a wheel of brahmin cheese once, entirely unprompted.

He said he'd 'acquired it from a surplus caravan.' I didn't ask from where. I distributed it to a squatter camp south of the Strip.

I believe in mercy before judgement. In his case, I find mercy comes easily.

The old ghoul. Erich.

He has been in this world longer than most faiths have been practised. When I met him he was reading something — an old poem, or a prayer, I couldn't tell the difference.

He told me his faith, if it existed, was in 'the stubbornness of living things.' I told him that was close enough to where I start every morning.

Barney Black. He has a lot of energy.

He asked me once if I thought war was God's punishment or God's test. I said I thought it was mostly a failure of imagination on humanity's part.

He considered this for a full minute, then said 'Interesting hypothesis. I will test it in the field.' I'm not sure that was the takeaway I was hoping for.

The woman at the farmstead. DOLORES.

I have prayed beside that farmhouse. She watches. She doesn't speak much. She sweeps.

What I feel standing there is not theological certainty. It is something older than that — the sense of a life that wants to continue but doesn't know how.

I don't have an answer for that. I have only company. I try to offer it.

emotional_nodes.text:
You are hurt and you are trying to pretend you aren't. I've been watching people do that for a long time.

Come here. I have stimpaks from the last supply drop. I don't need them right now and you clearly do.

The Lord helps those who help themselves, but He also apparently approves of stimpaks. The evidence is circumstantial but consistent.

You don't have much.

I have a little more than I need right now. Here — some caps and some food.

Not charity. An investment in the principle that what goes around eventually comes around. The pre-war people called it karma. Close enough.

quest_nodes.text:
There is a settlement south of Boulder City. Small. Maybe thirty people. They were doing well six months ago — water purifier, crops, a working generator.

Three weeks ago they stopped responding to radio contact. I was the only one making contact, so I'm probably the only one who noticed.

I need to go there. But I am not a fighter and the road through that stretch has become dangerous — a band of Fiends moved into the area after the NCR pulled a patrol post.

I'm asking for an escort. Not to fight unless necessary. Just to make sure I get there.

If the settlement is in trouble, I want to help. If it isn't — well. Sometimes you just need to see for yourself that people are all right.
quest_nodes.video_speech: A settlement south of Boulder City — thirty people — went quiet six months ago. I need someone to find out why. I can't go alone.

wildcards.text:
Faith is — and I know how this sounds out here — mostly about what you do when there's no good reason to do the right thing.

Anybody can be decent when it's easy. The interesting question is what you do when it costs you something.

The bombs didn't change that question. They just made it louder.

People ask me if I think the bombs were God's judgment.

I think they were human judgment. I think every civilization gets to make that choice, eventually — whether to extend itself or consume itself. We consumed ourselves.

What comes after is not punishment. It's consequence. And consequence, unlike punishment, can still be worked with.

This Bible survived the bombs because it was in a lead-lined display case in a museum. Preserved for historical value, not spiritual significance.

I found it and decided: both.

I've annotated the margins with wasteland survival notes. Leviticus is mostly water purification now. Proverbs has a section on rad avoidance. The Song of Solomon remains as written. Some things don't need updating.

The Church of the Atom. Yes.

We've had long conversations, their elders and I. They believe radiation is divine. I believe the divine encompasses radiation along with everything else.

The difference is mainly one of emphasis. We've agreed not to argue about it in front of settlers who are trying to have a normal day.

The Followers of the Apocalypse are the closest thing the wasteland has to my people's tradition of monastic medicine.

No oaths of poverty, obviously — you can't help anyone if you're starving — but the impulse is the same. Knowledge should be freely shared. Healing should not have a price tag.

I work with them when I can. Good people with a difficult mission.

fallback.text:
Safe travels, stranger. And if they're not safe — well.

That's what the stimpaks are for.
fallback.video_speech: Safe travels, stranger. And if they're not safe — well. That's what the stimpaks are for.
